concepts.title: Tables, Keys, and Relationships
concepts.description: Relational databases model the world as independent tables linked by keys; primary keys uniquely identify rows, foreign keys enforce relationships between tables, and normalization organizes columns to eliminate redundancy and the update anomalies it causes.
learningObjectives: Explain what a primary key is and why every table should have one.
Explain the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key, and when to prefer each.
Model a one-to-many relationship with a foreign key, and a many-to-many relationship with a junction table.
Explain the anomalies that 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF each eliminate, and identify violations in a sample schema.
Explain why normalization trades query simplicity for redundancy elimination, and when deliberate denormalization is reasonable.

sections.heading: Tables, Rows, and the Idea of a Primary Key
sections.body:
A relational database organizes data into tables: a table is a named collection of rows that all share the same set of typed columns. Conceptually a table is a two-dimensional grid, but the property that makes it *relational* is that tables can reference each other by value, not by memory address or physical position. That lets you model real-world relationships (an order belongs to a customer, a post has many comments) without duplicating whole records everywhere they're needed.

Every table you design should have a **primary key**: one column (or a small set of columns, a *composite* primary key) that uniquely identifies each row and can never be NULL. PostgreSQL enforces both halves of that guarantee automatically: declaring a column PRIMARY KEY creates a UNIQUE constraint and a NOT NULL constraint on it in one step, and backs it with a B-tree index for fast lookups (the mechanics of that index are the subject of the next module). Without a primary key, there is no reliable way to say 'update *this* row'. If two rows happen to be identical on every column you're filtering by, an UPDATE or DELETE with a matching WHERE clause affects both of them, not just the one you meant.

```sql
CREATE TABLE authors (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
```

`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the modern, SQL-standard way to get an auto-incrementing integer primary key in PostgreSQL (older code you'll encounter uses the `SERIAL` pseudo-type, which does the same job through a sequence, but `IDENTITY` is preferred in new code because the sequence belongs to the column for permission purposes, and an accidental explicit value is rejected unless you write `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`). A key like this one, with no meaning outside the database and invented to identify the row, is called a **surrogate key**. The alternative is a **natural key**: an existing real-world attribute that already happens to be unique, like an email address. Natural keys look appealing because they avoid an 'extra' column, but values you assumed were stable and unique sometimes aren't (emails get reused after an account is deleted, external identifier schemes turn out to have edge cases), and changing a primary key's value after other tables hold foreign keys pointing at it is far more disruptive than changing a column that's merely UNIQUE. The common, pragmatic default is a surrogate key as the primary key, plus a UNIQUE constraint on whatever natural key exists. You get fast lookups on both, and the stability of a key that nothing else depends on for its *meaning*. A `BIGINT` identity is compact and keeps inserts at the right edge of the primary key index. If you need ids that can be generated outside the database or exposed in URLs, a `UUID` works too, but fully random UUIDs scatter inserts across the whole index, which costs write performance on large tables.

sections.heading: Foreign Keys: Modeling One-to-Many Relationships
sections.body:
A **foreign key** is a column (or set of columns) in one table that must match a value already present in another table's primary key (or unique) column, or be NULL if the column allows it. This is how relational databases model a **one-to-many** relationship: one author can have many posts, so the 'many' side (`posts`) holds a foreign key column pointing back at the 'one' side (`authors`).

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    author_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
```

The database now *enforces* this relationship for you: PostgreSQL refuses an INSERT or UPDATE on `posts` that sets `author_id` to a value absent from `authors.id`, and it applies whichever `ON DELETE` policy you chose whenever someone tries to delete a referenced author. `ON DELETE RESTRICT` refuses to delete an author who still has posts, forcing you to decide what happens to those posts first. `ON DELETE CASCADE` would instead delete all of that author's posts automatically the instant the author row is deleted. That is convenient, but one DELETE on a parent row can fan out and remove a large amount of child data you didn't have in view at the call site. `ON DELETE SET NULL` is a third common option, useful when the child row should survive without its parent (an order shouldn't vanish just because the referring account was deleted). It only works if the foreign key column is nullable. One more thing to know: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced primary key but not the referencing column, so `posts.author_id` has no index until you create one. Without it, every delete of an author has to scan `posts` to check for children, and joins from author to posts get slower as the table grows.

sections.heading: Many-to-Many Relationships Need a Junction Table
Normalization: Naming the Anomalies It Prevents
sections.body:
**Normalization** is the discipline of organizing columns into tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. It's usually taught as a numbered sequence of 'normal forms,' but the numbers matter far less than the anomalies each one eliminates. Learn to recognize the anomaly in a schema and you can look up the definition later. In practice, a design that reaches 3NF has dealt with nearly all of the redundancy that causes bugs; the higher forms (BCNF, 4NF) matter mainly for tables with several overlapping candidate keys or independent multi-valued facts.

Imagine a single wide `orders` table with columns `order_id, customer_email, customer_name, product_name, quantity`. This is unnormalized, and it produces three classic problems: an **update anomaly** (if a customer changes their display name, you must find and update *every* order row they've ever placed, and missing even one leaves the data self-contradictory); an **insertion anomaly** (you can't record a new customer at all until they place an order, because 'customer' isn't a first-class row anywhere on its own); and a **deletion anomaly** (deleting a customer's only order accidentally erases every fact you knew about them as a customer, since nothing about them exists independent of that order row).

**First normal form (1NF)** requires every column to hold a single, atomic value: no comma-separated lists stuffed into one text column, no repeating groups of columns like `phone1, phone2, phone3`. Wanting a variable number of values in one field is a signal you need a separate, related table instead. **Second normal form (2NF)** matters when a table has a *composite* primary key, and requires every non-key column to depend on the *whole* key, not just part of it. A table keyed on `(order_id, product_id)` shouldn't also store `customer_email`, because that depends only on `order_id`, not on the product at all. **Third normal form (3NF)** requires non-key columns to depend *only* on the primary key, not on each other -- in the wide orders table above, `customer_name` depends on `customer_email` (itself a non-key column), and only through it on `order_id`. That transitive dependency causes the update anomaly. The fix is to split `customers` into its own table (`id, email, name`) and have `orders` reference it by `customer_id`. A customer's name now lives in exactly one row, and changing it is a single UPDATE that every order automatically reflects, because orders no longer store the name at all, only a reference to it.

sections.heading: Denormalization Is a Deliberate Trade-off, Not a Beginner Shortcut
sections.body:
Normalizing eliminates redundancy, but it also means some questions require joining several tables back together, which costs query complexity and, at scale, execution time. **Denormalization**, storing some redundant or derived data to avoid a join or a recomputation, is a legitimate engineering tool, but reach for it *after* you have a normalized model and a measured reason to deviate from it, not because joins seem inconvenient while you're still designing the schema.

A safer, more contained form of denormalization in PostgreSQL is a **materialized view**: write a normal, correct query, potentially an expensive one that joins several tables and aggregates, and `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_sales AS SELECT ...` stores its *result* physically, like a table, which you then query cheaply. The cost is that the view goes stale the moment the underlying tables change, and you're responsible for refreshing it (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_sales`) on whatever schedule your staleness tolerance allows. You can drop the view and lose nothing. Denormalizing the base schema, say by adding a redundant `customer_name` column back onto `orders` 'for speed', is much harder to undo: it brings back the update anomaly, with consistency now resting on every piece of code that ever writes an order.

examples.title: Foreign Key Enforcement in Action
examples.explanation: The second INSERT is rolled back because PostgreSQL checks the foreign key at the end of the statement, regardless of which code path issued it. An orphaned reference (a post pointing at an author that doesn't exist) can't survive the statement that tries to create it. Contrast that with an application that tries to 'be careful' by validating in code before every insert: a bug in one code path, a direct database script, or a second service writing to the same table can all bypass that validation, but none of them can bypass a foreign key constraint, because every write passes through the database. The DETAIL line names the offending value and the table it was missing from, which you would otherwise have to reconstruct by hand. One surprise: the failed insert still consumed a sequence number, so the next successful post gets id 3, not 2. Identity values are unique, not gap-free.

examples.title: The Composite Primary Key Blocks Duplicate Tag Assignments
examples.explanation: Because the primary key is the *pair* `(post_id, tag_id)` rather than either column alone, PostgreSQL treats the whole pair as the thing that must be unique. Many rows can share `post_id = 1` with different tags, but the second `(1, 1)` collides with the row already there. Notice also what `ON DELETE CASCADE` buys here that it didn't in the authors/posts example: deleting post 1 will automatically remove its rows from `post_tags` with no error and no orphaned junction rows left behind, which is correct because a `post_tags` row means nothing without the post and tag it links. An author's posts are records in their own right and deserve a human decision before being cascade-deleted.

examples.title: The Update Anomaly on Two Rows
examples.explanation: In the unnormalized table, `customer_name` is transitively dependent on `customer_email`, a non-key column, rather than on the primary key `order_id`. That is the root cause: the same name is copied onto every row that shares an email, so an UPDATE targeting one row leaves every sibling row stale unless you remember to chase down all of them by hand. The normalized version removes the whole category of bug, because `orders` no longer has a `customer_name` column to go stale in the first place. Everything that needs her name reads it from one `customers` row via the foreign key.

misconceptions.description: A table doesn't strictly need a primary key as long as the application code is careful to only ever write unique values.
misconceptions.clarification: A convention enforced only in application code is a habit that a single bug, a hand-run database script, a bulk import, or a second service writing to the same table can violate without the database objecting at all. It gets worse under concurrency: two simultaneous inserts can each check 'does this value already exist?' and both see 'no' before either one has committed, then both insert the supposedly-unique value. A database-level UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint closes that race, because the check and the insert happen atomically inside the database. A primary key is also the thing other tables' foreign keys point at. Without one (or a UNIQUE constraint), there is no guaranteed-unique target for a relationship to reference.
misconceptions.fact: A convention enforced only in application code is a habit that a single bug, a hand-run database script, a bulk import, or a second service writing to the same table can violate without the database objecting at all.

misconceptions.description: Normalizing all the way to 3NF is always strictly better, so any duplicated-looking data in a schema is automatically a design mistake.
misconceptions.clarification: Normalization targets redundancy that risks going *out of sync*: a value that's supposed to always match its single source of truth, copied in multiple places where an update to one copy can be forgotten on another. Not all repeated-looking data fits that description. A shipment record that snapshots 'the warehouse address at the time this shipment went out' is duplicating warehouse data on purpose, and it should NOT update if the warehouse later moves. For a historical record the snapshot is the correct model. Ask: is this value supposed to track its source going forward, or does it intentionally represent a fact frozen at a specific point in time? Only the first case needs normalizing.
misconceptions.fact: Normalization targets redundancy that risks going *out of sync*: a value that's supposed to always match its single source of truth, copied in multiple places where an update to one copy can be forgotten on another.

exercises.prompt: Design the schema for a many-to-many relationship between students and courses, where each enrollment also needs to record a grade, a fact that belongs to the student-course pairing rather than to either side alone. Write the CREATE TABLE statements.
exercises.code:
-- Write CREATE TABLE statements for: students, courses, and an
-- enrollments table linking them, including a grade column.
hints: A plain foreign key column can only point at one row on the other side: it can express 'many courses per student' or 'many students per course,' but not both directions at once.
The junction table needs its own row per (student, course) pairing. Since grade belongs to that pairing, it lives as a column on the junction table itself, not on students or courses.
The junction table's primary key should be the pair of foreign key columns together, which also enforces 'a student can't enroll in the same course twice.'
exercises.solutionExplanation: `enrollments` is the junction table: its composite primary key `(student_id, course_id)` guarantees a student can only have one enrollment row per course. `grade` is left nullable on purpose, because a student can be enrolled before a grade exists, and it lives here rather than on `students` or `courses` because a grade is a fact about the *pairing*, not about the student in general (they have a different grade in every course) or the course in general (different students get different grades). `ON DELETE CASCADE` on both foreign keys is appropriate for the same reason it was for post_tags, though a registrar who must keep transcripts would choose RESTRICT on `course_id` so that dropping a course can't erase grades.

exercises.prompt: This schema has an anomaly: a warehouse's address is duplicated onto every shipment row, so updating a warehouse's address after it relocates requires updating every historical shipment row too -- something nobody reliably remembers to do, and the requirement here really is 'always show the warehouse's current address,' not a historical snapshot. Identify the anomaly and rewrite the schema to fix it.
exercises.code:
CREATE TABLE shipments (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    warehouse_address TEXT NOT NULL,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    shipped_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
hints: Ask which table warehouse_address depends on: is it a fact about this shipment, or a fact about the warehouse, copied onto every shipment that happens to use it?
If a warehouse relocates, how many rows currently need to change to reflect that correctly? A normalized design should need one.
Pull warehouse_name and warehouse_address into their own table, keyed by an id, and reference it from shipments with a foreign key.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `warehouse_address` was transitively dependent on `warehouse_name` (not the primary key of `shipments`), the 3NF violation behind this update anomaly: the same address string is copied onto every shipment that used that warehouse, so moving the warehouse means finding and updating every one of those rows, and missing any leaves the schema self-contradictory about where that warehouse is. After the fix, a warehouse's address is stored in one row in `warehouses`; every shipment references it by `warehouse_id`, so an address change is a single UPDATE that every shipment automatically reflects. This fix is only correct because the stated requirement is 'always show the current address.' If the actual business need were a customs or audit record of 'the address the warehouse had at the time it shipped this order,' snapshotting the address onto the shipment row would be the *correct* design. Normalize based on what the data is supposed to mean, not by reflex.

assessments.prompt: A `products` table has no declared PRIMARY KEY, but the application always writes a unique SKU into every row. Why is relying on this convention riskier than declaring a PRIMARY KEY (or UNIQUE constraint)?
options: PostgreSQL requires every table to have a primary key just to physically store rows on disk, so a table without one silently fails to save data.
It isn't actually risky -- uniqueness enforced in application code is exactly as reliable as a database constraint, just implemented in a different layer.

Without a database-enforced constraint, a race condition between two concurrent inserts -- or a single application bug -- can create duplicate or NULL SKUs that the database accepts without complaint, and other tables have no guaranteed-unique value to reference via foreign key.
The only real downside is slightly slower SELECT queries, since primary keys exist purely to speed up reads.
assessments.explanation: The database checks the constraint atomically on every write, closing off both the concurrent-race case (two inserts each passing an app-level 'is this unique?' check before either commits) and the simple-bug case (a code path that forgets to check at all). It also gives other tables something dependable to point a foreign key at. The “PostgreSQL requires every table to have…” option is false; tables without a primary key store rows just fine but lack the uniqueness/not-null guarantee. The “It isn't actually risky -- uniqueness enforced…” option ignores that application-level checks can be raced or bypassed in ways a database constraint cannot. The “The only real downside is slightly slower…” option understates the risk (this is a correctness problem) and treats primary keys as if they existed only for reads.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'normalization is just an academic exercise -- in the real world you denormalize for performance anyway, so why bother getting the normalized model right first?' Explain what's wrong with this framing, and describe when denormalizing is actually a reasonable engineering choice.
assessments.modelAnswer: Normalization and denormalization solve different problems. Normalization's purpose is correctness: it eliminates redundancy that would otherwise let the same fact be stored in multiple places and go out of sync, producing update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. Skipping it costs you data integrity immediately, in the form of bugs where two rows disagree about a fact that should have one unambiguous answer, discoverable only when someone notices the inconsistency, often much later and often in production. Denormalization, when warranted, is layered *on top of* a correct, normalized model as a measured and ideally reversible optimization of an observed bottleneck, such as a materialized view that caches an expensive join-and-aggregate query and is refreshed on a known schedule, or a read replica serving traffic away from the primary. Used in place of a correct model, it brings the anomalies back, and every future piece of code that writes to the schema has to remember to keep the duplicated data consistent with no constraint to enforce it. The right sequence is: model correctly, measure, and only then denormalize the thing that measurement justifies.

assessments.prompt: An `orders` table declares `customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT`. What happens when someone tries to DELETE a customer row that still has orders referencing it?
options: The DELETE succeeds, and every order referencing that customer is deleted along with it.
The DELETE succeeds, and every order referencing that customer has its customer_id set to NULL automatically.
The DELETE succeeds for the customer row only, leaving orders rows whose customer_id points at a row that no longer exists.
The DELETE is rejected with a foreign key violation error.
assessments.explanation: RESTRICT refuses the delete and leaves the referencing rows alone, so a human or a piece of code has to decide first whether the orders should be reassigned, deleted, or nulled out. The “The DELETE succeeds, and every order referencing that customer has…” option describes ON DELETE SET NULL, and the “The DELETE succeeds, and every order referencing that customer is…” option describes ON DELETE CASCADE. Both are valid policies in PostgreSQL, but neither is what RESTRICT does. The “The DELETE succeeds for the customer row…” option describes the orphaned-reference state a foreign key exists to prevent, which is why the constraint is enforced at delete time as well as at insert/update time.

assessments.prompt: A table `order_items` has composite primary key `(order_id, product_id)` and also stores a `product_name` column copied from the products table. Which normal form does this violate?
options: No normal form is violated -- product_name is a normal descriptive column and is fine to store here.
2NF, because product_name depends only on product_id -- part of the composite key -- not on the whole key (order_id, product_id) together.
1NF, because product_name does not hold an atomic value.
3NF, because product_name depends on a non-key column rather than on the primary key.
assessments.explanation: 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key, not just part of it. Here, product_name is the same for every order that includes that product, so it depends only on product_id, which is the partial dependency 2NF forbids. The “1NF, because product_name does not hold an atomic value” option is wrong because product_name is a single atomic string; 1NF isn't the issue. The “3NF, because product_name depends on a non-key…” option describes a transitive dependency between two non-key columns, which isn't what's happening here (product_name depends on half of the primary key, not on another non-key column of order_items). The “No normal form is violated -- product_name…” option ignores that this redundancy is what causes an update anomaly: if a product's name changes, every order_items row referencing that product needs to be updated, or the data becomes self-contradictory.

assessments.prompt: A team runs `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_sales AS SELECT ...` to speed up an expensive report. Months later, someone notices the report doesn't reflect orders placed in the last week. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The materialized view stores a physical snapshot of the query's result as of whenever it was last refreshed.
PostgreSQL refreshes every materialized view automatically once every 24 hours, so the server must have been down for over a week.
Materialized views silently drop any rows inserted after their creation, so this is expected, permanent behavior that a refresh cannot fix.
Materialized views automatically stay synchronized with their underlying tables, so this must be a bug in the original query.
assessments.explanation: A regular view re-runs its query on every SELECT. A materialized view stores the query's result physically, like a table, so reading it is cheap, but that stored result goes stale the moment the underlying tables change, and staying current requires someone or something to run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW on a schedule matching the staleness the application can tolerate. The “Materialized views automatically stay synchronized with their…” option describes a regular view, not a materialized one. The “PostgreSQL refreshes every materialized view automatically once…” option invents an automatic refresh schedule that PostgreSQL does not provide by default; refreshing has to be scheduled (a cron job, pg_cron, or application logic). The “Materialized views silently drop any rows inserted…” option is wrong because a refresh does fix it.

concepts.title: Querying with SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY
concepts.description: SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY are the working core of SQL; understanding the logical order in which they execute, rather than the order you type them in, explains most of the surprising behavior beginners run into.
learningObjectives: Write SELECT queries that filter rows with WHERE using comparison, boolean, and pattern-matching operators.
Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN, and predict which rows survive each when a match is missing.
Use GROUP BY with aggregate functions to compute per-group summaries.
Explain why HAVING, not WHERE, is required to filter on an aggregate result.
Explain the logical order in which a SELECT query's clauses actually execute, and use it to predict what a query will and won't allow.

sections.heading: SELECT and WHERE: Choosing Columns and Rows
sections.body:
A SELECT query does two conceptually separate jobs: choosing which *columns* to return (projection, the SELECT list) and choosing which *rows* to return (filtering, the WHERE clause). WHERE operates on the rows produced by FROM/JOIN before the SELECT list is computed, so you can filter on a column you don't even include in the SELECT list.

```sql
SELECT title, published_at
FROM posts
WHERE author_id = 1
  AND published_at IS NOT NULL;
```

WHERE supports the comparison operators you'd expect (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`), boolean combination with `AND`/`OR`/`NOT`, set membership with `IN (...)`, range checks with `BETWEEN ... AND ...`, and pattern matching with `LIKE` (case-sensitive) or PostgreSQL's `ILIKE` (case-insensitive), where `%` matches any run of characters and `_` matches exactly one. A sharp edge: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, just as multiplication binds tighter than addition in arithmetic, so `WHERE status = 'active' OR status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false` does NOT mean 'active or pending, as long as not flagged'. It means 'active (regardless of flag), OR (pending AND not flagged),' because the AND clause groups first. Parenthesize whenever you mix AND and OR: `WHERE status = 'active' OR (status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false)`.

sections.heading: JOIN: Combining Rows Across Tables
sections.body:
A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a matching condition. The most common form, `INNER JOIN`, keeps only the rows that have a match on both sides. Conceptually, it's as if PostgreSQL paired up every row from the left table with every row from the right table, then kept only the pairs satisfying the `ON` condition.

```sql
SELECT authors.name, posts.title
FROM authors
INNER JOIN posts ON posts.author_id = authors.id;
```

If an author has zero posts, they don't appear in this result: there's no row on the `posts` side to pair them with. That's often what you want, but if the question is 'list every author, and their posts if they have any,' you need `LEFT JOIN`, which keeps every row from the left table regardless of whether a match exists on the right, filling in NULL for every right-side column when there's no match.

```sql
SELECT authors.name, posts.title
FROM authors
LEFT JOIN posts ON posts.author_id = authors.id;
```

An author with no posts now appears once, with `posts.title` as NULL, instead of vanishing. `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image (keep every row from the right table, NULL-fill the left), but it's rarely used: almost anything you'd write with RIGHT JOIN reads more naturally as a LEFT JOIN with the two table names swapped, so most style guides standardize on LEFT JOIN.

sections.heading: GROUP BY and Aggregates: Collapsing Rows into Summaries
sections.body:
`GROUP BY` collapses multiple rows sharing the same value(s) in specified column(s) down into one summary row per group, and it's almost always paired with an **aggregate function** (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) that computes something across all the rows in each group.

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

This produces one row per distinct `customer_id`, with `order_count` and `total_spent` computed across that customer's own orders. PostgreSQL enforces a strict rule here that trips up people coming from more permissive databases: every column named in the SELECT list that *isn't* wrapped in an aggregate function must also appear in the GROUP BY list. (The one exception: if you group by a table's primary key, you may select its other columns too, because the key determines them.) `SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` raises an error, because `order_date` isn't aggregated and isn't grouped on. For a customer with three orders on three different dates, PostgreSQL has no principled way to decide which `order_date` the one summary row should display, so it refuses to guess. Two related habits help here: `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` counts each value once, and you can group by an expression, such as `GROUP BY date_trunc('month', order_date)`, to summarise per month.

sections.heading: HAVING vs WHERE: Filtering Before vs After Aggregation
sections.body:
Filtering on an aggregate with WHERE doesn't work: `SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 3 GROUP BY customer_id` fails outright. The reason is about *when* each clause conceptually runs: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation has happened, so when WHERE is evaluated there's no group yet to count. `HAVING` filters *after* grouping and aggregation, where an aggregate result is available to test:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
```

WHERE decides which *rows* make it into the grouping; HAVING decides which *groups* survive into the final result. You can combine both in one query: WHERE to cheaply discard rows you never want considered at all (say, `WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'`), and HAVING to filter on what the surviving rows aggregate to per group.

sections.heading: The Logical Order of a SELECT Query
sections.body:
SQL's written clause order doesn't match its logical execution order, and knowing the logical one resolves most 'why doesn't this work' confusion. (It is a model of the result; the planner is free to run things in another order if the answer is the same.) Logically, a query executes roughly as: **FROM/JOIN** (build the combined row set) -> **WHERE** (filter individual rows) -> **GROUP BY** (collapse into groups) -> **HAVING** (filter groups) -> **SELECT** (compute the output columns/expressions) -> **DISTINCT** -> **ORDER BY** -> **LIMIT/OFFSET**.

It explains why WHERE can't use an aggregate but HAVING can (GROUP BY hasn't happened yet when WHERE runs). It explains why you can't reference a column alias defined in the SELECT list from within the WHERE clause in the same query (`SELECT price * quantity AS total FROM orders WHERE total > 100` fails in standard SQL, because WHERE executes before SELECT computes `total`), yet you can reference that alias in ORDER BY, which runs after SELECT. And it explains why LIMIT without ORDER BY gives you an *arbitrary* subset of rows, not 'the first N inserted': LIMIT is the last step, cutting an unordered result set at a boundary that means nothing without a preceding ORDER BY to make 'first N' well-defined.

examples.title: Operator Precedence: Why AND/OR Need Parentheses
examples.code:
-- Intent: active accounts, or pending accounts that aren't flagged
SELECT id, status, is_flagged
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'active' OR status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false;

-- What it actually means (AND binds tighter than OR):
SELECT id, status, is_flagged
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'active' OR (status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false);

-- What was probably intended:
SELECT id, status, is_flagged
FROM accounts
WHERE (status = 'active' OR status = 'pending') AND is_flagged = false;
examples.explanation: The first query includes every flagged 'active' account, because the AND binds only to the 'pending' branch and `status = 'active'` stands on its own. The bug is dangerous because the query runs without error and returns a plausible-looking result set. The second query adds parentheses that change nothing, to make the grouping visible. The third is what was wanted ('active or pending, and not flagged in either case'), and it needs parentheses around the OR to override AND's tighter binding.

examples.title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: What Happens to Unmatched Rows
examples.code:
-- authors: (1, 'Amara Chen'), (2, 'Ben Osei' -- has zero posts)
-- posts:   (1, 'Intro to SQL', author_id=1)

SELECT authors.name, posts.title
FROM authors
INNER JOIN posts ON posts.author_id = authors.id;
-- Amara Chen  | Intro to SQL
-- (Ben Osei does not appear at all)

SELECT authors.name, posts.title
FROM authors
LEFT JOIN posts ON posts.author_id = authors.id;
-- Amara Chen | Intro to SQL
-- Ben Osei   | NULL
examples.explanation: INNER JOIN only keeps combined rows where the ON condition is satisfied. No row in `posts` has `author_id = 2`, so there is no pairing for Ben Osei to appear in, and he's dropped from the result with no error or warning. LEFT JOIN instead guarantees every row from the left table (`authors`) survives into the result regardless of whether a match exists on the right, substituting NULL for every column that would have come from the unmatched right-hand side. Choosing the wrong one is a common bug: if your question is 'how many authors have never published anything,' an INNER JOIN can never answer it, because authors with no matching posts are the rows it excludes before you get a chance to filter on them.

examples.title: GROUP BY with HAVING: Customers With More Than 3 Orders
examples.code:
-- This fails: WHERE cannot reference an aggregate.
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 3
GROUP BY customer_id;
-- ERROR:  aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE

-- This works: HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
examples.explanation: When WHERE is evaluated, rows haven't been grouped yet, so `COUNT(*)` has no group to count over. The second query fixes this by moving the aggregate filter to HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY has formed the per-customer groups and computed `COUNT(*)` for each one. The WHERE clause still does useful work in the corrected version: `order_date >= '2026-01-01'` throws out rows before grouping, which is both correct (those orders shouldn't count toward this year's total) and more efficient than aggregating first and discarding groups afterward.

misconceptions.description: WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable ways to filter a query -- just use whichever one comes to mind first.
misconceptions.clarification: They filter at different logical stages. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping, so it cannot reference an aggregate's result. HAVING filters already-formed groups after GROUP BY and aggregation have run, and it's the only clause that can test an aggregate like `COUNT(*)` or `SUM(...)`. A query can use both together: WHERE to cheaply exclude rows before they're even grouped, HAVING to filter on what the surviving rows aggregate to.

misconceptions.description: INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN return the same rows as long as every row on the left happens to have a match on the right today, so it doesn't really matter which one you default to using.
misconceptions.clarification: That's true only for the data you currently have, which makes it a fragile assumption rather than a property of the query. The moment a new row is inserted on the left side without a corresponding match on the right (a customer who hasn't placed an order yet, an author who hasn't published yet), an INNER JOIN drops that row, while a LEFT JOIN keeps it with NULLs. Use INNER JOIN when a match is required for the row to make sense in the output, and LEFT JOIN when the left-side row is meaningful on its own and an absent match is part of the answer. The two also interact with filters. Put a condition on the right-hand table in the `ON` clause (`LEFT JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = a.id AND p.published_at IS NOT NULL`) and authors without published posts still appear with NULLs. Put the same condition in `WHERE` and the NULL rows are filtered out, so the LEFT JOIN quietly behaves like an INNER JOIN.

exercises.prompt: Given `authors: (1, 'Amara'), (2, 'Ben')` where Ben has no rows in `posts`, and `posts: (1, 'Intro to SQL', author_id=1)`, what does each of these two queries return?
hints: INNER JOIN only keeps combined rows where a match exists on both sides. What happens to a left-side row with no match at all?
LEFT JOIN guarantees every row from the left table appears at least once, filling in NULL for right-side columns when there's no match.
Work out whether Ben appears in each query's result, and if so, what posts.title shows for him.
exercises.expectedAnswer: INNER JOIN: one row, ('Amara', 'Intro to SQL') -- Ben is excluded entirely because he has no matching post. LEFT JOIN: two rows, ('Amara', 'Intro to SQL') and ('Ben', NULL) -- Ben survives because LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL.
exercises.solutionExplanation: INNER JOIN conceptually pairs every authors row with every posts row and keeps only the pairs where `posts.author_id = authors.id` holds true. Since no row in `posts` has `author_id = 2`, there is no pair involving Ben at all, so he's absent from the result rather than shown with a NULL. LEFT JOIN instead starts from 'keep every row in authors, no matter what,' and only uses the ON condition to decide what (if anything) to attach from posts. Amara matches normally and gets her post's title attached. Ben has no match, so his row still appears, but every column that would have come from `posts` is NULL, since there's no post row to pull a title from.

exercises.prompt: This query is meant to list customers who have placed more than 3 orders, but it fails to run at all. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 3
GROUP BY customer_id;
hints: Think about the logical order a SELECT query executes in -- does grouping and aggregation happen before or after WHERE is evaluated?
COUNT(*) is an aggregate computed per group. At the point WHERE runs, have any groups been formed yet?
There's a specific clause designed to filter on an aggregate's result, evaluated after GROUP BY.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
exercises.solutionExplanation: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY forms any groups and before any aggregate function has a group to compute over, so `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` asks PostgreSQL to compare against a value that doesn't exist yet at that stage of execution, which is why it errors outright rather than just returning an unexpected result. HAVING runs after GROUP BY and aggregation, so by then `COUNT(*)` has been computed for each customer and HAVING can keep only the groups where it exceeds 3.

assessments.prompt: An `orders` table has some rows referencing `customer_id` values that don't exist in `customers` (perhaps from a data migration issue). A query does `SELECT customers.name, orders.id FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id`. What happens to orphaned orders rows?
options: They are silently excluded from the result, because INNER JOIN only keeps rows that have a match on both sides.
They appear in the result with customers.name shown as NULL.
The query raises a foreign key violation error, since the join condition can't be satisfied.
They appear once for every row in customers, since INNER JOIN falls back to a full cross join when no match exists.
assessments.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only combined rows that satisfy the ON condition. An orphaned order produces no satisfying pair, so it's dropped from the output with no error and no NULL placeholder. The “They appear in the result with customers.name…” option describes LEFT JOIN's behavior, not INNER JOIN's. The “The query raises a foreign key violation…” option is wrong because a JOIN is a read-time operation with no relationship to whether a foreign key constraint exists or was ever enforced; an unmatched join condition is a normal outcome. The “They appear once for every row…” option describes a cross join with no ON condition at all, which is a different operation.

assessments.prompt: Explain the logical order in which a SELECT query's clauses execute, as opposed to the order you type them in, and use it to explain why an aggregate like COUNT(*) can be used in HAVING but not in WHERE.
assessments.modelAnswer: Although you write a SELECT statement in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, that is not the order in which the database evaluates it. Logically, execution proceeds roughly as: FROM and any JOINs first build the combined set of candidate rows; WHERE then filters those individual rows down, one at a time, with no knowledge of any grouping yet; GROUP BY then collapses the surviving rows into groups based on the specified columns; HAVING filters those already-formed groups, typically based on an aggregate computed over each one; SELECT then computes the output columns and expressions (which is why you can't reference a SELECT-list alias inside WHERE); and finally ORDER BY and LIMIT sort and truncate the finished result. An aggregate like COUNT(*) only has a value once rows have been grouped, and WHERE executes before that step begins. HAVING executes after GROUP BY has formed groups and the aggregates have been computed per group, so it can filter on the result.

assessments.prompt: Which rows does `WHERE status = 'active' OR status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false` actually return?
options: A syntax error, because PostgreSQL refuses to evaluate AND and OR in the same WHERE clause without explicit parentheses.
Rows where status is 'active' regardless of is_flagged, or status is 'pending' and is_flagged is false.
Rows where all three conditions -- active, pending, and not flagged -- must simultaneously be true, which is impossible.
Rows where status is 'active' or 'pending', and additionally is_flagged is false in both cases.
assessments.explanation: AND binds tighter than OR, so the AND clause groups first: the expression parses as `status = 'active' OR (status = 'pending' AND is_flagged = false)`. That means every 'active' row is included whatever its is_flagged value, while 'pending' rows are only included if they're also unflagged. The “Rows where status is 'active' or 'pending'…” option describes what the query would mean if OR bound tighter, or if it were written with parentheses around the OR. The “A syntax error, because PostgreSQL refuses…” option is wrong: mixing AND and OR without parentheses is legal SQL, just easy to misread. The “Rows where all three conditions -- active…” option misreads the clause as requiring all three conditions at once, which isn't how OR works.

assessments.prompt: Why does `SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` raise an error in PostgreSQL?
options: COUNT(*) cannot be combined with GROUP BY in the same query.
customer_id must itself be wrapped in an aggregate function, such as MIN(customer_id), before it can appear in GROUP BY.

order_date appears in the SELECT list but is neither wrapped in an aggregate function nor included in GROUP BY, so PostgreSQL has no principled way to choose a single order_date value to display for a customer with multiple orders on different dates.
GROUP BY requires every column in the table's schema to be listed, not just the ones actually being grouped on.
assessments.explanation: PostgreSQL enforces a strict rule: every column in the SELECT list that isn't inside an aggregate function must also appear in GROUP BY. order_date satisfies neither condition here, and for a customer with orders on several different dates, there is no single correct order_date value to show on that customer's one summary row, so PostgreSQL raises an error. The “COUNT(*) cannot be combined with GROUP BY…” option is false; COUNT(*) is the aggregate most often used with GROUP BY. The “GROUP BY requires every column…” option invents a requirement that doesn't exist; only columns that appear ungrouped and unaggregated in the SELECT list (or HAVING or ORDER BY) matter. The “customer_id must itself be wrapped…” option is backwards: customer_id is the GROUP BY column and is fine as written.

assessments.prompt: In standard SQL, `SELECT price * quantity AS total FROM orders WHERE total > 100` fails, but referencing `total` in an ORDER BY clause on the same SELECT works fine. Why the difference?
options: This is a bug specific to PostgreSQL; the SQL standard requires both clauses to see the alias identically.
Aliases are only valid inside numeric contexts, and WHERE is considered a boolean context while ORDER BY is not.
WHERE clauses are restricted to plain column references and cannot contain any computed expression, regardless of aliasing.
WHERE executes before SELECT computes its output expressions, so the alias `total` doesn't exist yet at that point; ORDER BY executes after SELECT, once `total` is a real, computed output column.
assessments.explanation: The logical order of execution is FROM/JOIN, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY. WHERE runs before SELECT has computed any output expressions, so there is no `total` to compare with 100. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, once every output column exists, so referencing `total` there works. The “Aliases are only valid inside numeric contexts…” option invents a distinction between 'numeric' and 'boolean' contexts that has nothing to do with the real cause. The “This is a bug specific to PostgreSQL…” option is wrong: this behavior follows from the standard's execution order. The “WHERE clauses are restricted to plain column…” option is false; WHERE can filter on computed expressions, such as `WHERE price * quantity > 100` written out instead of through an alias.

concepts.title: Constraints and NULL Semantics
concepts.description: Constraints let the database enforce business rules on every write regardless of which code path performs it, while NULL's three-valued logic (true, false, or unknown) changes how comparisons, boolean logic, and aggregates behave in ways that catch almost every SQL beginner at least once.
learningObjectives: Use PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, and NOT NULL constraints to enforce data integrity at the database level.
Explain why NULL represents 'unknown' rather than a normal value like zero or an empty string.
Predict the outcome of comparisons and boolean expressions involving NULL, including inside WHERE clauses.
Explain why NULL values are excluded from most aggregate calculations, and why COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) can differ.
Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL correctly, and explain why `= NULL` never matches any row.

sections.heading: Constraints as Enforced Business Rules
sections.body:
A constraint is a rule the database checks on every write, regardless of which application, script, or person is doing the writing. You've already seen PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null) and FOREIGN KEY (must reference an existing row). `UNIQUE` is the same uniqueness guarantee as a primary key, without the not-null requirement and without being the table's single main key, which suits secondary uniqueness rules like an email address or a SKU. A nullable UNIQUE column accepts any number of NULLs by default, because two NULLs don't count as equal (PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to change that). `NOT NULL` forbids NULL in a column; apply it wherever 'unknown' isn't a valid state for your application.

`CHECK` takes an arbitrary boolean expression over the row. A row is rejected when the expression is FALSE; one that evaluates to NULL passes, which is why a CHECK is usually paired with NOT NULL.

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
    sku TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
```

A row with a negative `price` is rejected the instant anything tries to write it, whether that's a careful application, a careless one-off migration script, or a typo in an ad-hoc UPDATE run against production. No piece of code has to remember the check. Name your constraints too (`CONSTRAINT non_negative_price CHECK (price >= 0)`): the name appears in the error message, and a later migration that drops or replaces the rule can refer to it. Constraints can also be added to an existing table with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT`, but PostgreSQL then checks every existing row, and one violating row makes the statement fail.

sections.heading: NULL Means Unknown, Not Empty or Zero
sections.body:
NULL is easy to misread as one more possible value, 'the empty one.' An empty string `''` is a known value: a string containing zero characters. The number `0` is a known value too. NULL means the value is *unknown*, *missing*, or *not applicable*.

A `middle_name` column holding `''` is asserting a known fact: this person has no middle name (or an empty one, depending on your domain rules). The same column holding NULL says we don't know their middle name, or it doesn't apply to them. Collapsing the two throws away information you may need, for example when deciding whether to prompt the user for it.

sections.heading: Three-Valued Logic: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN
sections.body:
Because NULL means 'unknown,' any comparison involving it produces a third logical value, UNKNOWN. `age = 30` where `age` is NULL doesn't evaluate to FALSE (which would claim to know the age isn't 30); it evaluates to UNKNOWN. This propagates: `5 = NULL` is UNKNOWN, `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN (two unknowns aren't necessarily equal to each other), and any arithmetic touching NULL (`NULL + 1`) produces NULL.

WHERE (and HAVING, and JOIN ON conditions) keep a row only when its condition evaluates to TRUE, so UNKNOWN excludes the row just as FALSE does. `SELECT * FROM people WHERE age != 30` looks like it should return 'everyone whose age isn't 30, obviously including anyone with an unknown age, since an unknown age certainly isn't confirmed to be 30', but it doesn't. Every row where `age` is NULL evaluates `age != 30` to UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN rows get filtered out alongside the FALSE ones. To include rows with an unknown age, ask for them: `WHERE age != 30 OR age IS NULL`, or PostgreSQL's shorthand `WHERE age IS DISTINCT FROM 30`. Other clauses treat NULLs by their own rules: `DISTINCT` and `GROUP BY` put all NULLs together as one value, and `ORDER BY` sorts them last in ascending order and first in descending order unless you add `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST`.

sections.heading: The NOT IN / NULL Trap and Other Footguns
sections.body:
The NULL bug that does most damage involves `NOT IN` against a subquery whose results might contain a NULL. `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT banned_id FROM banned_ids)` is logically equivalent to a chain of `id <> x1 AND id <> x2 AND id <> x3 ...` for every value the subquery returns. If even *one* of those values is NULL, that one comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN, and `AND`'s truth table says TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so the chain can never come out TRUE. An id that is on the list still gives FALSE, every other id gives UNKNOWN, and WHERE drops both: the query returns **zero rows**, with no error to alert you.

The robust fix is `NOT EXISTS`, which asks 'does at least one matching row exist?' A NULL row doesn't match, and so has no effect:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM banned_ids b WHERE b.banned_id = u.id
);
```

`COALESCE(expression, fallback)` is the standard tool for defaulting a NULL when you want 'unknown' treated as some known value for a calculation, e.g. `COALESCE(discount_percent, 0)` to treat a missing discount as zero instead of letting NULL spread through the rest of the expression.

sections.heading: NULL and Aggregates: Why COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) Differ
sections.body:
`SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, and `COUNT(column)` all ignore NULL values. `COUNT(*)` counts *rows*, whatever the columns contain. (`array_agg` and `json_agg` are exceptions on the other side: they keep NULLs as elements.) When every input is NULL or there are no rows, `COUNT(column)` returns 0 but `SUM` and `AVG` return NULL.

```sql
-- people: (1, age=25), (2, age=NULL), (3, age=35)
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(age), AVG(age) FROM people;
-- COUNT(*) = 3   (all three rows exist)
-- COUNT(age) = 2 (only two rows have a known age)
-- AVG(age) = 30  (25 + 35) / 2, NOT (25 + 0 + 35) / 3
```

`AVG(age)` is the average of the *known* ages: the NULL row is left out of both the sum and the divisor. (psql displays it as `30.0000000000000000`, because AVG over integers returns `numeric`.) That's right for ages, where an unknown shouldn't drag the average toward zero. For something like units sold per day, where no row value may mean none sold, you'd want `AVG(COALESCE(units, 0))`, which turns the NULLs into zeros before the aggregate sees them.

examples.title: CHECK and UNIQUE Constraints Rejecting Bad Data
examples.explanation: Neither rejected insert leaves a row behind, and each error names the constraint and the offending value, so an application can catch the violation and map the constraint name to a user-facing message. The CHECK constraint states a rule particular to this domain (`price >= 0`) once, in the schema, instead of in every code path that can produce a `products` row.

examples.title: Why `WHERE column = NULL` Never Matches
examples.explanation: `age = NULL` asks the operator `=` to compare `age` with NULL, which evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, including the row where age is NULL. WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, so this query returns nothing and raises no error. `IS NULL` is a separate predicate that tests for NULL and always answers TRUE or FALSE. The bug often arrives through a bind parameter: `WHERE age = $1` with a null argument matches nothing.

examples.title: The NOT IN NULL Trap
examples.explanation: The NOT IN version expands, conceptually, to `email <> 'spam@example.com' AND email <> NULL` for every user row. For Amara, the first comparison is TRUE (her email isn't the spam one), but the second comparison, against the stray NULL row, is UNKNOWN. TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so her row is filtered out even though she's not on the banned list. The query raises no error, and the cause sits in another table's data, so nothing in the WHERE clause looks wrong. NOT EXISTS only asks whether a matching row exists, and a NULL in `banned_emails` never matches anyone's email.

misconceptions.description: NULL is basically the same as an empty string or zero -- it's just a way of saying a column has 'no value.'
misconceptions.clarification: An empty string and zero are known values (a string of length zero, and the number zero), and comparisons or arithmetic against them behave like those against any other known value. NULL means the value is unknown, missing, or not applicable, and that changes the semantics of everything touching it: `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN (not TRUE), `NULL + 1` is NULL, and aggregate functions skip NULLs rather than treating them as zero. Treating NULL as 'the empty version of a value' leads to bugs like assuming `WHERE age != 30` includes people with an unknown age, or assuming `AVG(price)` treats a NULL price as a zero-cost item. Neither is true.
misconceptions.fact: An empty string and zero are known values (a string of length zero, and the number zero), and comparisons or arithmetic against them behave like those against any other known value.

misconceptions.description: `WHERE column = NULL` is a normal comparison that matches rows where the column happens to be NULL, the same way `WHERE column = 5` matches rows where the column is 5.
misconceptions.clarification: SQL's three-valued logic makes any `= NULL` comparison evaluate to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE for every row, including rows where the column is NULL. WHERE only keeps rows whose condition is TRUE, so `column = NULL` returns zero rows whatever the data. Test with `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL` instead.

exercises.prompt: Given the table `people` with rows `(1, age=25), (2, age=NULL), (3, age=35), (4, age=NULL)`, what does this query return?
exercises.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(age) AS known_ages, AVG(age) AS avg_known_age
FROM people;
hints: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of what any column contains. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is NOT NULL.
AVG(age) is computed only over the rows where age is known: NULLs are excluded from both the sum and the divisor, not treated as zero.
Work out how many rows have a known age, and what their sum and average are, ignoring the two NULL rows.
exercises.expectedAnswer: total_rows = 4, known_ages = 2, avg_known_age = 30. COUNT(*) counts all four rows regardless of NULLs. COUNT(age) only counts the two rows where age is not NULL (rows 1 and 3). AVG(age) computes (25 + 35) / 2 = 30, ignoring the two NULL-age rows: it does not divide by 4, and does not treat the NULLs as zero.
exercises.solutionExplanation: COUNT(*) counts rows unconditionally, so it reports 4 regardless of which columns contain NULL. COUNT(age), by contrast, only counts rows where age is NOT NULL, so rows 2 and 4 are excluded, leaving 2. AVG(age) sums only the known ages (25 + 35 = 60) and divides by the count of known ages (2), giving 30. Treating NULL as zero would have given 60 / 4 = 15.

exercises.prompt: This query is meant to find all users whose email is not on the banned_emails list, but it's returning zero rows even though most users clearly aren't banned. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
-- banned_emails contains ('spam@example.com') and one bad row (NULL),
-- accidentally inserted by a broken import script.

SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email NOT IN (SELECT email FROM banned_emails);
hints: NOT IN expands, conceptually, into a chain of `email <> x` comparisons ANDed together for every value the subquery returns. What does AND do when one of those comparisons is UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE?
One of the values NOT IN is comparing against is NULL. What does `email <> NULL` evaluate to, for every user?
There's a different construct that checks whether a matching row exists, rather than comparing against every individual value.
exercises.solutionExplanation: NOT IN against a subquery is logically equivalent to ANDing together an `email <> value` comparison for every value the subquery returns. Because one of those values is NULL, the comparison `email <> NULL` evaluates to UNKNOWN for every user. TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN and FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE, so the condition is never TRUE for anyone, hence zero rows. NOT EXISTS only asks whether at least one row in banned_emails matches this user's email, and a NULL row never does. Adding NOT NULL to banned_emails.email would stop the import script from creating the bad row in the first place.

assessments.prompt: A `people` table has some rows where `age` is NULL. What does `SELECT * FROM people WHERE age != 30` return, with respect to those NULL-age rows?
options: It excludes every NULL-age row, because `age != 30` evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE) when age is NULL, and WHERE only keeps rows whose condition is TRUE.
It includes NULL-age rows only if there is also at least one row where age actually equals 30.
It raises an error, because you cannot compare a NULL column using != without first checking IS NOT NULL.
It includes every NULL-age row, since an unknown age is certainly not confirmed to equal 30.
assessments.explanation: Any comparison against NULL, including !=, evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE filters UNKNOWN rows out just as it does FALSE ones. The “It includes every NULL-age row, since…” option describes the intuitive but incorrect expectation that unknown values default to satisfying inequality checks; SQL doesn't infer 'unknown but definitely not 30'. The “It raises an error, because you cannot…” option is wrong because the comparison is syntactically and semantically legal; it just doesn't do what you might hope. The “It includes NULL-age rows only if there…” option is wrong because the presence or absence of other rows has no bearing on how a given row's own comparison evaluates.

assessments.prompt: Explain why NOT IN can produce zero rows without an error when its subquery includes a NULL, and why NOT EXISTS avoids this trap. Use three-valued logic in your answer.
assessments.modelAnswer: SQL's NOT IN against a subquery is logically equivalent to a chain of inequality comparisons, `x <> v1 AND x <> v2 AND x <> v3 ...`, one for every value v the subquery produces. In SQL's three-valued logic any comparison involving NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, because a comparison against an unknown quantity can't be answered either way. If even one of the subquery's returned values is NULL, the corresponding comparison `x <> NULL` evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row being tested, no matter what x actually is. Under AND's truth table, TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN and FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE, so once an UNKNOWN comparison enters the chain the expression can never be TRUE: rows that match a listed value give FALSE and all others give UNKNOWN. WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, so the query returns zero rows with no error. NOT EXISTS asks an existential question instead: does at least one row in the subquery match this row, by whatever join condition you specify? EXISTS itself returns only TRUE or FALSE, and a NULL row in the subquery never satisfies an equality match, so it has no effect on the answer.

assessments.prompt: A `products` table declares `price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0)`. A buggy application later issues `UPDATE products SET price = -10 WHERE id = 5`. What happens?
options: PostgreSQL silently clamps the value to 0 instead of storing the out-of-range -10.
The UPDATE is rejected with a constraint violation error.
The UPDATE succeeds, but PostgreSQL writes a warning to the server log that must be checked manually afterward.
The UPDATE succeeds silently, because CHECK constraints are only evaluated on INSERT, never on UPDATE.
assessments.explanation: A CHECK constraint is enforced on every write that would produce a failing row, INSERT and UPDATE alike. The “The UPDATE succeeds silently, because CHECK constraints…” option is a common but incorrect assumption. The “The UPDATE succeeds, but PostgreSQL writes…” option invents a behavior PostgreSQL doesn't have; a CHECK violation is an error that aborts the statement. The “PostgreSQL silently clamps the value to 0…” option invents a clamping behavior that doesn't exist; PostgreSQL rejects the write and leaves the existing row untouched.

assessments.prompt: Table `people` has rows `(1, age=25), (2, age=NULL), (3, age=35)`. What does `SELECT SUM(age), COUNT(age) FROM people` return?
options: SUM = NULL, COUNT = 3 -- the presence of any NULL makes the entire SUM undefined.
SUM = 60, COUNT = 3, because COUNT(column) always behaves identically to COUNT(*).
SUM = 60, COUNT = 2 -- both SUM and COUNT(age) ignore the NULL row entirely.
SUM = 60, COUNT = 3 -- SUM ignores the NULL when totaling, but COUNT(age) counts every row regardless of NULLs.
assessments.explanation: SUM(age) and COUNT(age) both skip rows where age is NULL when computing their result. SUM adds only the known ages (25 + 35 = 60), and COUNT(age) counts only the rows where age is NOT NULL, which is 2 (rows 1 and 3), not 3. The “SUM = 60, COUNT = 3 -- SUM ignores the NULL…” and “SUM = 60, COUNT = 3, because COUNT(column)…” options both incorrectly claim COUNT(age) counts all rows, which is the behavior of COUNT(*), not COUNT(column). The “SUM = NULL, COUNT = 3…” option invents a 'NULL poisons the whole aggregate' behavior that doesn't apply here; NULL spreads through `+` and through chained comparisons like NOT IN, but SUM skips NULL inputs.

assessments.prompt: The `manager_id` column in `employees` has a NOT NULL constraint, guaranteeing `SELECT manager_id FROM employees` can never return a NULL value. Is `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)` safe to use here, or should it still be rewritten as NOT EXISTS?
options: It's safe only if the outer column, id, also carries a NOT NULL constraint.
It's unsafe regardless of the NOT NULL constraint, because NOT IN is deprecated in PostgreSQL and no longer guaranteed to execute correctly.
It's unsafe because NOT IN always performs a slow sequential scan, independent of any constraint on the underlying column.
It's safe specifically because the NOT NULL constraint guarantees the subquery can never return a NULL.
assessments.explanation: The NOT IN/NULL trap depends on the subquery's *result set* containing a NULL: once one comparison in the ANDed chain is UNKNOWN, the chain can't be TRUE. A NOT NULL constraint on manager_id guarantees the subquery never produces that NULL, so NOT IN behaves as you'd expect here. The “It's unsafe regardless of the NOT NULL…” option is false: NOT IN isn't deprecated, it's risky when its subquery can contain NULL. The “It's unsafe because NOT IN always performs…” option is a performance claim, and an overstated one (PostgreSQL often hashes the subquery's result, though it can't plan NOT IN as an anti join the way it can NOT EXISTS); the question is about correctness. The “It's safe only if the outer column…” option is wrong because a NULL id would drop only its own row; it's a NULL in the subquery's result that empties the output for every row.
